svg.title: Why the tiled kernel needs two __syncthreads per tile
svg.text: Why the tiled kernel needs two __syncthreads per tile
two warps of one block sharing one tile; time runs left to right (schematic, not measured)

g.text: Both barriers present. Each warp loads its half of tile t; warp 1 is slower (its loads missed in cache).
Each warp loads only its own cells: cooperation means nobody has the whole tile alone.
Warp 0 reaches barrier 1 (line 93) and WAITS. It cannot start the inner loop on a half-filled tile.
Barrier 1 = "everyone has WRITTEN the tile". Released only when the last thread arrives.
Both compute on the complete tile. Warp 0 finishes first and waits at barrier 2 (line 98).
Barrier 2 = "everyone has finished READING the tile". Only then may anyone overwrite it.
Then both load tile t+1. Correct every time, whatever the timing.
Cost of the two barriers: the fast warp idles (grey). That idle time is why later kernels double-buffer.
REMOVE barrier 1: warp 0 starts its inner loop while warp 1 is still writing its half.
Warp 0 reads warp 1's cells before they are written: it multiplies tile t−1 (or garbage) values. Wrong C.
REMOVE barrier 2: warp 0 finishes tile t and immediately overwrites its half with tile t+1.
Warp 1 is still reading row values from warp 0's half: it now mixes tile t and t+1. A race: wrong only SOMETIMES.
Early return before a barrier: a guard thread that returns never arrives at __syncthreads.
Undefined behaviour (hang or wrong). So the tiled kernels load 0.0f out of range and guard only the store (line 100).
